title: What is a custom ThreadFactory and why would you write one? How do you set thread names, daemon status, priority, and an UncaughtExceptionHandler, and how do you pass it to a ThreadPoolExecutor?

s1_definition.profdef: A `ThreadFactory` is a single-method factory interface (`Thread newThread(Runnable r)`) that an `ExecutorService` calls every time it needs to create a worker thread. The default factory produces threads named `pool-N-thread-M`, non-daemon, with normal priority and no uncaught-exception handler. A custom `ThreadFactory` lets you control four things at creation time: a meaningful name prefix so thread dumps are readable, the daemon flag so pool threads do not block JVM shutdown, the priority, and an `UncaughtExceptionHandler` so a task that throws outside the Future path still gets logged instead of dying silently.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India hires temporary clerks for the settlement counter. The default HR process gives them no name badge, no shift rule, and nobody to report accidents to. A custom ThreadFactory is a proper onboarding desk: every new clerk gets a badge like `settlement-pool-thread-3`, is marked as a temp who must leave when the branch closes (daemon), is given a priority level, and is told exactly whom to call if something blows up (UncaughtExceptionHandler). When a manager later reviews CCTV (a thread dump), every clerk is identifiable.
s1_definition.oneliner: A custom ThreadFactory names, flags, prioritizes, and attaches a crash handler to every pool thread at birth — pass it to the ThreadPoolExecutor constructor so observability starts before the first task runs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `ThreadFactory` is a single-method factory interface (`Thread newThread(Runnable r)`) that an `ExecutorService` calls every time it needs to create a worker thread. The default factory produces threads named `pool-N-thread-M`, non-daemon, with normal priority and no uncaught-exception handler. A custom `ThreadFactory` lets you control four things at creation time: a meaningful name prefix so thread dumps are readable, the daemon flag so pool threads do not block JVM shutdown, the priority, and an `UncaughtExceptionHandler` so a task that throws outside the Future path still gets logged instead of dying silently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India hires temporary clerks for the settlement counter. The default HR process gives them no name badge, no shift rule, and nobody to report accidents to. A custom ThreadFactory is a proper onboarding desk: every new clerk gets a badge like `settlement-pool-thread-3`, is marked as a temp who must leave when the branch closes (daemon), is given a priority level, and is told exactly whom to call if something blows up (UncaughtExceptionHandler). When a manager later reviews CCTV (a thread dump), every clerk is identifiable.

**One line to remember:** A custom ThreadFactory names, flags, prioritizes, and attaches a crash handler to every pool thread at birth — pass it to the ThreadPoolExecutor constructor so observability starts before the first task runs.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a settlement pool that processes end-of-day trades for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001). One night the service froze. The on-call engineer took a thread dump and saw only `pool-1-thread-1` through `pool-1-thread-8`. Nobody could tell which pool those threads belonged to, because the reporting service and the audit service also used anonymous pools. Hours were wasted. This is exactly what a custom ThreadFactory fixes: by naming threads `settlement-pool-thread-N`, the next dump instantly shows which subsystem is stuck.

Problem 2 — A background cache-refresh pool kept the JVM alive during a deploy because its threads were non-daemon. The deploy script hung for two minutes every release. Marking those threads daemon lets the JVM exit cleanly.

Problem 3 — A settlement task threw a `NullPointerException` from inside an `execute` call (not `submit`), so no Future captured it. The exception printed to stderr, which was not wired to the log aggregator, so the failure was invisible until a customer complained. An UncaughtExceptionHandler attached by the factory logs every such escape with the thread name.

The code builds a `BankThreadFactory` (name prefix, daemon flag, priority, handler), a `SettlementService` that submits settlement tasks to a pool built from that factory, and a demo that settles two trades and deliberately throws once to prove the handler fires.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a fixed pool of size 2 built from `BankThreadFactory("settlement-pool", false)`, plus two settle requests for SAV2001 (Rs.50,000 and Rs.30,000) and one faulty request.

Step 1: The pool needs its first worker, so it calls `factory.newThread`. The factory increments the counter to 1 and produces a thread named `settlement-pool-thread-1`, non-daemon, with an attached handler. The thread is still only created lazily when the first task arrives.

Step 2: The first settle task runs on `settlement-pool-thread-1`. It calls `debit(50000)`, so SAV2001 moves from Rs.1,000,000 to Rs.950,000, and logs the thread name.

Step 3: The second settle task needs a worker; the pool creates `settlement-pool-thread-2` through the same factory. It debits Rs.30,000, so the balance goes from Rs.950,000 to Rs.920,000.

Step 4: The faulty task runs via `execute`, throws `IllegalStateException`, and because no Future captured it, the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler fires and logs "Uncaught exception in settlement-pool-thread-N" with the stack trace. The pool replaces that dead worker for future tasks.

Step 5: `shutdown` lets running tasks finish; `awaitTermination` waits. Final balance Rs.920,000 is logged.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: settlement-pool-thread-1 settled Rs.50000 on SAV2001
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: settlement-pool-thread-2 settled Rs.30000 on SAV2001
Oct 21, 2026 ... SEVERE: Uncaught exception in settlement-pool-thread-1
java.lang.IllegalStateException: corrupt trade record
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Final balance for SAV2001 = Rs.920000
```

    │                     ├─ setPriority(NORM)
    │                     └─ setUncaughtExceptionHandler(log.severe)

  │ settlement-pool-thread-1  │ settlement-pool-thread-2   │

  UncaughtExceptionHandler → LOG.severe("Uncaught in settlement-pool-thread-N")
                  │
                  ▼
  shutdown() + awaitTermination() → Final balance Rs.920,000
```

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        BankThreadFactory              │
  │  - prefix: String                     │
  │  - daemon: boolean                    │
  │  - counter: AtomicInteger             │
  │  + newThread(r): Thread               │  sets name/daemon/priority/handler
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                  │ used by
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        SettlementService              │
  │  - pool: ExecutorService              │  ◇ aggregation
  │  + settle(acct, amount): void         │  submit()
  │  + settleFaulty(): void               │  execute() → handler path
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for newThread(r):
    Pre:  r != null
    Post: returns configured Thread, counter incremented
    Guarantees: unique name, handler attached

  Thread lifecycle: NEW → RUNNABLE → (TERMINATED | crash→handler→replaced)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A ThreadFactory is the single-method factory that an executor service calls whenever it needs to create a worker thread. The default factory gives you threads named pool-something-thread-something, non-daemon, with normal priority and no crash handler. I write a custom factory whenever a pool runs in production, because there are four things I want to control at the exact moment a thread is born: its name, whether it is a daemon, its priority, and its uncaught exception handler.

The most important of those is the name. When a service stalls in production, the first thing I do is take a thread dump, and a dump full of anonymous names tells me nothing. If instead every worker is named settlement-pool-thread-three, I immediately know which subsystem is saturated and which one is stuck. So in my factory I keep an atomic counter and name each thread with a meaningful prefix followed by the thread number, which is the same convention the JDK uses, just with a prefix that identifies the subsystem.

The daemon flag matters for clean shutdown. For a background pool like a cache refresher I set the threads daemon so they never block the JVM from exiting during a deploy, whereas for a batch that must finish I keep them non-daemon. Priority I set but never rely on, because the operating system treats it as a weak hint. The uncaught exception handler is my safety net: exceptions from submit are captured in the Future, but exceptions that escape from an execute call or from the thread itself would otherwise print to standard error and disappear, so the handler logs them with the thread name.

At National Bank of India I used exactly this on the settlement pool. We build the pool from a BankThreadFactory that names every worker settlement-pool-thread-N, keeps them non-daemon because end-of-day settlement must complete, and attaches a handler that logs any escape to our aggregator. The first time a corrupt trade record threw outside the Future path, the handler caught it and told us precisely which worker died, and the pool quietly replaced it. The one line I give interviewers is that a custom ThreadFactory makes observability start before the first task runs, because you name, flag, and protect every worker at the moment of its creation.
